I think the BJP is misdiagnosing the challenge it faces with younger Indians.

The assumption seems to be that this is primarily a communication problem: more Instagram reels, more vertical video, younger lingo, a different style of addressing people.

But that is a first-order response to a much deeper shift on the ground.

Gen Z does not necessarily want political leaders to imitate its language or aesthetic. In fact, trying too hard to do so can make leadership look less authentic.

The problem is not style. It is content.

PM Modi’s great political strength over the last 25 years has been his ability to combine remarkable continuity with constant reinvention: the core remains identifiable, but every few years there is a sense of a new mission.

That was also supported by decades of ideological clarity within the broader ecosystem on issues such as Article 370, Ram Mandir and the UCC.

Many of those longstanding objectives are now either accomplished or substantially advanced.

So the natural question is: what is the next big agenda?

For younger India, I would put three issues near the top. They relate emotionally and intellectually to these 3 issues. Addressing them will naturally connect the BJP with them. 

1. Urban governance

For far too long, Indians have accepted cities that are congested, polluted, poorly planned and increasingly difficult to live in.

The Smart Cities Mission had the right ambition, even if its outcomes were uneven. That happens with governments and large programmes.

Now it needs a sharper second avatar.

The PM could identify perhaps 20–25 cities, bring together India’s best architects, urban planners and administrators, and make them demonstrable models of excellent municipal governance.

You do not need to transform every Indian city simultaneously. First create examples that prove it can be done—particularly in BJP-governed states.

2. Government school education

Anyone closely connected with ground realities knows the condition of many state government schools.

This has persisted for decades, across parties and governments, and India should no longer accept it as inevitable. It starts seriously with Nehru Ji- he is often blamed for ignoring school education.

Improving state schools should become a major national political ambition, pursued with willing state governments, measurable outcomes and clear deadlines. 

Again, a few states producing dramatically better results can establish a benchmark for the rest of India.

3. Environment and urban green spaces

This is both a quality-of-life issue and one that fits naturally with India’s civilisational emphasis on harmony with nature.

Cities need serious programmes for tree cover, neighbourhood green spaces and large urban “oxygen zones”—not merely symbolic plantation drives, but sustained ecological improvement.

These may sound like softer issues than national security, infrastructure or macroeconomics.

But they shape everyday life—and therefore shape how young Indians experience the country.

A young person may not distinguish between what is constitutionally the responsibility of the Centre, a state government or a municipality. When one political party governs across several of these levels, dissatisfaction inevitably travels upward.

That is why these issues should be taken head-on.

There is also a larger communication point.

Viksit Bharat 2047 is an important national horizon, but 2047 is psychologically very far away—especially for someone who is 20 today.

A long-term vision needs shorter missions within it: concrete national goals for 2030, 2032, 2035 and beyond.

People stay engaged when they can see milestones being crossed.

The next phase could also be presented as a natural progression from the first decade.

From 2014 onward, the focus was necessarily on foundational questions: national security, border infrastructure, highways and expressways, financial inclusion, housing, sanitation, basic economic architecture, digital infrastructure, the space sector and state capacity.

Much of that work must continue.

But the next chapter can increasingly focus on the quality of everyday Indian life:

Better cities.
Better schools.
Cleaner and greener neighbourhoods.

GoDaddy has challenged a Delhi High Court order that it says could reshape how the internet works far beyond India.

In December, the court blocked more than 1,100 fake websites impersonating brands like Amazon, McDonald's and Microsoft. But the ruling went further, issuing 14 directives that tech experts say rewrite the rules of internet governance. Domain sellers can no longer offer free privacy protection by default. A website owner's name, address, phone and email must be released to anyone with a "legitimate interest" within 72 hours. Domain names resembling protected brand names are prohibited outright.

GoDaddy, which manages 80 million domains for over 20 million customers, has filed a 5,121-page appeal arguing the order conflicts with India's own data protection law and the EU's GDPR. It warns the directives are commercially destabilising enough to force domain companies to exit India. Namecheap and Hosting Concepts have filed their own challenges.

India's concern is grounded in a real crisis. The government received 2.4 million cybercrime complaints last year involving losses of 2.4 billion dollars, and the Home Minister has said one person falls victim to cybercrime every 37 seconds. Court records show the directives closely followed submissions by the IT and home ministries.

Internet governance researchers warn the people exposed by public registration data will be journalists, activists and small business owners rather than fraudsters. GoDaddy points to a practical problem: protecting a trademark like HUL would overlap with 118 English words, including hulk and moghul.

A larger bench hears the appeals on July 16. A domestic anti-fraud ruling is quietly becoming a global internet governance precedent.

Source: Reuters

🛜 🌍 The world's biggest domain seller GoDaddy says India's fight against fake websites could make the internet less safe. A fight not many are watching,  but is set to reshape internet governance, we report at @Reuters 

🌍Let's understand the background -- India has a fake-website problem. For years, fraudsters have registered domains impersonating global brands -- bogus Amazon shopping sites, fake McDonald's franchise offers, phony Microsoft support pages -- to con ordinary people. Dozens of companies took them to court.

🌍 What happened in December 2025? a Delhi judge cracked down. She blocked more than 1,100 fraudulent sites. But she didn't stop there.

She wrote sweeping new rules for the entire domain industry: strip away privacy protection by default, hand over website owners' details within 72 hours to anyone claiming a "legitimate interest," and block any web address resembling a protected brand.

🌍 The big news now: Now GoDaddy -- which runs 80 million domains worldwide -- is fighting back in thousands of pages of court filings my colleagues and I reviewed . Its warning is striking: the rules would make the internet less safe, not more. They'd expose ordinary website owners to stalking and harassment. And because domain systems are global, an order from one Delhi courtroom could ripple across the entire web -- potentially forcing GoDaddy to "exit India" altogether.

🌍 They are colourful filings: One of GoDaddy's arguments? That you can't ban the word "McDonald" -- it's a Scottish surname meaning "son of the world ruler."  The U.S. giant also submitted research compiled from the Merriam-Webster's website to argue that safeguarding variations of a protected trademark like "HUL" - Unilever's Indian unit, could overlap with 118 English words that contain the string, like "hulk" and "moghul".

🌍 It's a landmark collision between a nation trying to protect its citizens and the borderless architecture of the internet itself.

Estimates of click rates on genuine phishing emails, as opposed to simulations, are lower than untrained simulation baselines and closer to a few percent. Proofpoint and related summaries have cited figures in the range of roughly 2.7 percent to 3.4 percent for real phishing clicks, depending on year and sample. Even a 3 percent click rate is large at inbox scale. If 100,000 people receive a campaign, 3,000 clicks is 3,000 potential credential or malware events. Attackers do not need a majority. They need a thin slice of a large list.Phishing is a form of social engineering in which an attacker sends a message designed to look like it comes from a trusted person or institution, then asks the recipient to take an action that benefits the attacker. The most common action is a click: a link, a button, an attachment, or a QR code that moves the recipient from a message they were already reading into an environment the attacker controls.The click is a small act. It is also the point at which a large share of subsequent harm becomes possible. Industry and government datasets do not treat that click as a rare event committed only by people who “should have known better.” They treat it as a recurring, measurable behavior that appears across countries, industries, job roles, and levels of technical skill. This article summarizes what those datasets and technical analyses show about volume, cost, timing, psychology, and what happens after the click. It does not sell products or training programs. It reports published figures and https://t.co/FFQyMgHqaw large the problem isThe Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG) counts unique phishing attacks reported by members and the public. In 2025 it recorded about 3.8 million unique phishing attacks, slightly above 3.76 million in 2024. Quarterly volume was not flat. Q1 2025 had 1,003,924 attacks. Q2 2025 reached 1,130,393, the highest quarter since Q2 2023. Q3 fell to 892,494. Q4 fell further to 853,244. In Q1 2026 the count rose again, to 971,181, a 13.8 percent increase from the previous quarter. Monthly totals inside that quarter were relatively even: 320,264 in January, 329,625 in February, and 321,292 in March. That pattern is consistent with industrialized production rather than a single https://t.co/6sPATOprJd.apwg.orgBrand targeting shifts by quarter. In early 2026, contributing APWG analysis identified telecom as the most frequently attacked sector at 33 percent of attacks, up from 5.9 percent in Q3 2025, with SaaS and webmail following at 20 percent. Earlier quarters had put finance, payments, SaaS/webmail, and social media near the top. The common feature is not a single industry. It is any brand whose login page, if copied, yields reusable identity: email, cloud suites, banks, shipping portals, telecom account pages.phisheye.comThose attack counts are not the same as emails sent. One “attack” in APWG terms is typically a unique phishing site or campaign instance. The number of messages is far larger. Microsoft has reported blocking on the order of billions of email-based phishing threats in a single quarter. Kaspersky reported that its anti-phishing systems blocked 554,002,207 attempts to follow fraudulent links in 2025, and that mail anti-virus blocked 144,722,674 malicious email attachments. Kaspersky also reported that 44.99 percent of emails observed worldwide in that period were spam. Spam and phishing are not identical. Spam is unsolicited bulk mail. Phishing is deceptive mail whose purpose is credential theft, malware delivery, or fraud. The two overlap in inboxes.securelist.comComplaint data from the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) measures something else: what victims reported in the United States. In 2025, IC3 received 1,008,597 complaints and $20.877 billion in reported losses, the first year of more than one million complaints and a 26 percent increase in losses from 2024. Phishing and spoofing were the most frequently reported crime type, with 191,561 complaints, about 19 percent of all complaints. Reported losses attributed specifically to phishing and spoofing were $215.8 million, up from $70 million in 2024. That increase in loss with relatively stable complaint volume means each reported incident was, on average, more expensive. Business email compromise (BEC), a related category that often begins with a phished or spoofed mailbox, accounted for 24,768 complaints and $3.046 billion in losses. Combined, phishing/spoofing and BEC were a large share of complaint volume and a large share of email-origin financial harm. IC3 figures are lower bounds. They include only what people reported.dmarcian.comBreach-cost studies measure organizational incidents rather than consumer complaints. IBM’s Cost of a Data Breach research for the 2025 report put phishing as the most common initial attack vector among studied breaches, at 16 percent, with an average cost around $4.8 million for phishing-initiated incidents. The 2026 edition, based on 602 organizations with breaches between March 2025 and February 2026, put the global average cost of a data breach at $4.99 million, up 12 percent from the prior year, and the U.S. average at $11.5 million. In that later dataset, phishing remained a leading initial vector. Voice and SMS phishing were associated with the highest average breach cost among vectors cited in secondary summaries of that report, at $5.29 million. Social engineering that impersonated help-desk or IT staff was associated with about $5.23 million. These are averages across studied organizations, not the cost of a single clicked link. A click that yields nothing further costs little. A click that yields a mailbox, a cloud tenant, or ransomware can cost https://t.co/Hz6VoXdyT9.comVerizon’s Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) analyzes confirmed incidents. In the 2026 edition, covering incidents from November 1, 2024 through October 31, 2025, the human element was present in 62 percent of breaches, a slight increase from 60 percent the prior year. Social engineering accounted for 16 percent of breaches. Phishing remained a large share of those social-engineering cases. Pretexting — a fabricated scenario used to extract action or information, often by voice — reached 6 percent of all breaches. For the first time in the report’s 19-year history, exploitation of vulnerabilities (31 percent) overtook stolen credentials as the leading initial access vector in the 2026 analysis. That does not mean phishing stopped working. It means vulnerability exploitation rose enough to take first place, while phishing, pretexting, and credential abuse continued to appear in a large minority of cases. Third-party involvement in breaches also rose.zdnet.comThe datasets disagree on ranking because they measure different things. APWG counts phishing sites and campaigns. IC3 counts U.S. victim reports. IBM surveys breach costs at organizations that experienced incidents. Verizon codes confirmed breaches. Kaspersky counts blocked attempts on its customer base. None of them is a census of every click on Earth. Together they show the same outline: phishing remains high-volume, identity-focused, expensive when it succeeds, and mixed with adjacent fraud such as BEC, smishing, and vishing.What a click is, technicallyA phishing email is a delivery wrapper. The payload is usually a URL, sometimes an attachment, sometimes a QR code that encodes a URL. The click is the moment the recipient’s client requests that resource.Several outcomes are common.First, a credential-harvesting page. The page copies the visual design of a bank, a cloud login, a payroll portal, a shipping company, or a government site. The recipient types a username and password. Those values are sent to the attacker, often through a form post to a collection panel, a Telegram bot, or email. Kaspersky analysis of campaigns from January through September 2025 found that 88.5 percent of observed phishing attacks sought account credentials, 9.5 percent sought personal data such as names and addresses, and 2 percent sought bank-card details. Stolen credentials are frequently aggregated, checked for validity, and resold. A single click can therefore feed later attacks that the original recipient never sees.me-en.kaspersky.comSecond, adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing. In this design the page is not only a fake form. It is a reverse proxy. The victim’s browser talks to the attacker’s server. The attacker’s server talks to the real login service in real time. The victim sees the genuine login flow, including multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts. Password, one-time code, and push approval all pass through the proxy. After the real service issues a session cookie or token, the proxy copies it. The victim may even land in a real-looking session. The attacker now has a live authenticated session and can replay the cookie from another machine. MFA that is tied to a one-time code or a push notification does not stop this, because the victim completed a real authentication. The control that fails is the assumption that “MFA means the session belongs only to the person who typed the code.” Session theft is the point. Commercial phishing-as-a-service kits have productized this pattern, including services that relay Microsoft 365 sign-ins and capture cookies after MFA. Published analyses of kits such as those in the Evilginx family, and later commercial offerings, describe the same relay: two TLS sessions, one to the victim and one to the real identity provider, with cookies harvested in the https://t.co/EvOPUvgB68.comThird, malware delivery. The click downloads an attachment or a file from a hosting site. Historically this included Office macros, password-protected archives, and executable droppers. More recent campaigns have used HTML smuggling, malicious scripts the user is instructed to paste into a system dialog (sometimes called ClickFix), and “fix your document” pages that ask the user to run a command. The email is still the lure. The click or the follow-on instruction is the execution step.Fourth, a benign-looking intermediate hop. Attackers often route victims through a legitimate service first: a shared document link, a URL wrapper used by an email security product, a cloud redirect, or a QR code printed in an email. The first destination may be clean at the moment the message is scanned. The second destination is the phishing site. This timing gap is why some filtered mail still produces clicks. The message that arrived looked wrapped or hosted on a known brand. The page that loaded later was not.Fifth, conversation rather than a single page. BEC and pretexting may not need a malicious domain at all. A compromised mailbox, or a lookalike domain, is used to continue an existing thread about invoices, wire instructions, or password resets. The “click” may be a reply, an attachment open, or a call-back number. Verizon’s 2026 analysis treated pretexting as a growing path into ransomware and extortion, often by voice after an initial email or chat https://t.co/DwOl5375tP all five cases the recipient’s action supplies something the attacker could not obtain from the public internet alone: a secret, a session, code execution, or a human decision inside a payments https://t.co/7rFASxtciw fast the click happensVerizon’s 2025 DBIR reported that the median time from opening a phishing email to clicking the link was 21 seconds. The median time to report the same class of message was 28 minutes. That gap is operationally large. If one person clicks at 21 seconds and another reports at 28 minutes, the attacker has tens of minutes of uncontested access in the median case. Secondary summaries of that dataset have also stated that among users who click, a substantial fraction go on to submit credentials. Exact submission rates vary by study and by whether the sample is a simulation or a live campaign.phishgrid.comTwenty-one seconds is not enough time to inspect a domain letter by letter, compare it with a bookmarked login, call the purported sender, or read an email header. It is enough time to recognize a familiar logo, a familiar subject line, and a button. That is the design goal of the lure: to fit inside the window of automatic reading.Simulation click rates and real-world click rates are different numbers. They should not be mixed.KnowBe4’s 2026 Phishing by Industry Benchmarking Report, based on simulated tests, put the global baseline “phish-prone percentage” — the share of employees who engaged with a simulated phish before training — at 33.2 percent. After 90 days of awareness training in that dataset the figure fell to 20.1 percent. After one year it fell to 4.2 percent. Large organizations started higher than small ones: 39.5 percent baseline for enterprises with 10,000 or more employees, versus 24.7 percent for organizations with fewer than 250 employees. Healthcare and pharmaceuticals (42.7 percent), insurance (38.1 percent), and retail and wholesale (36 percent) were the highest-risk industries at baseline for a second year. These numbers describe behavior on tests that employees may or may not recognize as tests. They do not prove that one in three employees clicks every real phish that arrives. They do show that, in the absence of repeated practice, a large minority fails a first simulated lure.knowbe4.comProofpoint’s simulation reporting has put average failure rates much lower in organizations that already run programs, around 4.93 percent across campaigns in one 2024–2025 dataset, with industry variation (legal services higher, energy and utilities lower in that sample). Reporting rates in the same family of studies have often been in the high teens as a baseline, with financial-services users reporting more often than education users. A click rate and a report rate are both necessary to interpret risk. A workplace that clicks 5 percent and reports 30 percent presents a different operational picture than one that clicks 5 percent and reports 2 percent.swif.aiVerizon’s 2026 simulation notes found median email simulation click rates around 1.4 percent in its sample, with mobile-centric simulations (voice and text) about 40 percent higher, near 2 percent. The non-email sample was small relative to the email sample. The direction of the finding is still used in the report: users were more likely to engage with social engineering on phones than with classic email lures in those tests. *STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

One Blocking Order Every 68 Seconds: When the State Starts Controlling the Digital Public Square

[The News Minute — 1.95 lakh blocking orders in five months]
https://t.co/4pKxvmx3EL

The number is staggering:

Nearly 1.95 lakh government blocking directions to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July 2026 — roughly one every 68 seconds. 

And there is an important caveat: 1.95 lakh blocking orders do not necessarily mean 1.95 lakh individual posts were removed. A single order can cover hundreds of posts, accounts or pieces of content. 

But even with that qualification, the scale demands serious democratic scrutiny.

The distribution is striking:

Instagram: nearly 1 lakh orders

Facebook: around 80,000

YouTube: nearly 15,000

Most were routed through the Union Home Ministry's Sahyog portal. Meta has also integrated its systems with the portal, allowing flagged material to be removed automatically in response to government directions. 

And the timing cannot simply be ignored.

These five months overlapped with the student protests over examination irregularities, during which social media became an important tool for mobilisation and public discussion. Reporting has also documented takedowns involving posts supporting the protests and criticism of government policies. 

There is another crucial legal distinction that must not be lost in the political debate:

These 1.95 lakh directions should not all be described as Section 69A blocking orders. A significant proportion were issued through Sahyog under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, which operates differently from Section 69A. 

That distinction makes the central democratic question even more important:

Who decides what citizens are allowed to see, question and share — and what independent mechanism exists to challenge that decision?

A democratic government unquestionably needs mechanisms to tackle deepfakes, fraud, cybercrime, incitement and genuinely unlawful content.

But those powers must come with transparency, due process, accountability and meaningful avenues of appeal.

Because social media is no longer merely entertainment.

It is where citizens organise, protest, educate one another, expose wrongdoing, criticise governments and participate in democracy.

When the machinery capable of silencing digital speech operates at the rate of one government blocking direction every 68 seconds, every citizen should be asking:

What is being blocked?
Why is it being blocked?
Who ordered it?
And who watches the people doing the blocking?

A democracy should never fear citizens who question power.

It should fear a system in which citizens become afraid to question it.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Beyond the Numbers: Why Pre-Colonial School Surveys Don’t Prove Caste Equality

​A popular argument on social media cites 19th-century British surveys (by Thomas Munro, William Adam, and Mountstuart Elphinstone) to claim that pre-colonial India was free from caste discrimination because many "Shudras" were found in village schools.

​This claim sounds convincing on the surface, but looking directly at the historical data reveals clear evidence of rigid caste discrimination.

​1. The Surveys Themselves Documented Exclusion
The argument that these surveys disprove casteism ignores what the reports actually found:

-​ The Sanskrit Monopoly: William Adam’s 1830s survey in Bengal and Bihar noted that while village pathshalas had diverse students, higher education institutions (tols and chatushpathis) were almost 100% upper-caste. They taught philosophy, law, and Sanskrit, and lower castes were barred from them.

- ​The Complete Absence of Dalits: In Thomas Munro’s 1826 Madras report, the total number of "Panchamas" (untouchable/Dalit castes) enrolled across hundreds of schools was close to zero. The "60–70% non-Brahmin" statistic largely represented intermediate farming and merchant castes, not untouchable communities.

​2. The Veranda Practice: Segregation Inside the Classroom

Even in the rare cases where Dalit or lower-caste children accessed a school, they were subjected to strict spatial untouchability:

- ​Dalit children were not allowed to sit on mats inside the classroom with upper-caste students.

- ​They were forced to sit outside in the veranda or courtyard, listening to the teacher from a distance so their physical presence or shadow would not "pollute" others.

- ​Teachers would avoid touching their slate or books, tossing educational materials onto the ground instead of handing them over.

​3. Jyotirao Phule’s Testimony to the Hunter Commission (1882)
If pre-colonial or 19th-century education had truly been egalitarian, there would have been no need for social reformers to fight for basic schooling access:

- ​In 1848, Mahatma Jyotirao Phule and Savitribai Phule had to open their own independent schools in Pune specifically because Dalits and lower-caste girls were banned from standard schooling.

- ​In 1882, Phule submitted official testimony to the British Hunter Commission, stating that government-funded schools were dominated by orthodox teachers who actively drove away lower-caste children or refused to teach them alongside upper-caste students.

​4. Occupational Literacy vs. Emancipatory Education
A village pathshala in 1820 was not an instrument for social equality:

- ​Dalit children were not allowed to sit on mats inside the classroom with upper-caste students.

- ​They were forced to sit outside in the veranda or courtyard, listening to the teacher from a distance so their physical presence or shadow would not "pollute" others.

- ​Teachers would avoid touching their slate or books, tossing educational materials onto the ground instead of handing them over.

The second-order effect argument sounds compelling in theory but falls apart against one simple question: we already have OBC creamy layer. Has it reduced reservations by a single percentage point? Has it generated any political momentum toward abolition? The answer is no. Creamy layer did not reduce OBC reservation. It just shuffled who gets it. That is the entire historical record we have, and it argues against your position, not for it.

Now to the arithmetic, because that is where this argument actually dies.

Take Chamars in UP. Their population is roughly 12%. Even if you accept the most generous assumption that successive generations of the same families have been cornering government jobs through reservation, you are talking about 5% of Indians being in government employment at any point. Apply that to Chamars and you get 0.6% of the population that could plausibly be called beneficiaries. Exclude every single one of them. The remaining Chamar population eligible for reservation is still 11.4%. You have not moved the needle. Ten poor Chamars are standing behind every rich one. No government is going to cut reservation on the argument that some members of a caste have become affluent while the vast majority remain poor.

Take Meenas, who are the loudest example used in this debate. Their pan-Indian population is roughly 0.5% of the total. Exclude every Meena from ST reservation tomorrow. Will the government reduce ST reservation from 7.5% to 7%? Of course not. That is not how this works and everyone knows it.

The best case scenario for creamy layer, assuming honest implementation, honest income certificates, and a tight threshold, which are all enormous assumptions given what we have seen with OBC creamy layer, is this: Dudhlal who retired from a bank job with a crore in pension benefits cannot pass reservation to his son. Instead Mangat Ram, who drives an auto or works as farm labour, gets it for his son. That is a genuine internal equity improvement within SC/ST communities. It is a worthy goal on its own terms. But it does not open one additional seat for General Category. It does not reduce reservation by one percent. It does not build political momentum toward abolition because the reserved population as a whole loses nothing.

Reform as a gateway to further reform only works if the first reform actually shrinks the pie. Creamy layer does not shrink the pie. It redistributes slices within the same communities. The political coalition that defends reservation remains exactly as large and exactly as motivated after creamy layer as before it.

text:
Catastrophic flash flood on the Nepal–Tibet border (Wednesday, 26 August 2026). A glacial collapse sent a wall of mud, rock, ice and water down the Bhote Koshi / Lhende Khola into the Trishuli river system, wiping out villages, a border crossing, roads, bridges and hydropower plants. It is one of Nepal’s deadliest disasters in years.

WHAT EXACTLY HAPPENED:

Around 8:40 a.m. local time, a sudden surge of debris-laden water tore through Rasuwa district (north of Kathmandu) near the Rasuwagadhi / Gyirong Port crossing, then raced downstream through Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan and other districts. Entire settlements and markets were buried or swept away. Videos from the Chinese side show people fleeing as a wall of mud hit the border post.

The USGS initially flagged a magnitude-4.4 earthquake but later determined there was no earthquake. The seismic signal came from the glacial collapse and debris flow itself. Satellite imagery points to an ice-and-rock landslide on the Tibetan side that temporarily dammed the river before the dam burst. Experts have warned of a possible second surge from remaining blocked water upstream.

Casualties (as of Thursday 27 August — still rising)
Confirmed dead: at least 165 (Nepal police recovered ~157–162 bodies; China reports 3 dead in Gyirong). Officials expect the toll to climb as searches continue.

MISSING: 

nearly 1,500 people across both countries.
-Nepal: ~826 unaccounted for (including ~500 foreigners / hundreds of tourists).
-Tibet (Gyirong county): 558 missing, including 260 foreigners.

Foreign nationals reported missing (figures vary slightly by source and are being updated):
-India: 142–177 (many Kailash–Mansarovar pilgrims)
-United States: 47–63
-Australia: 34
-United Kingdom: 33
-Canada: 24–25
Also: South Koreans (hydropower workers), Malaysians, and others from more than two dozen countries.

Locals, 28 Nepalese police, soldiers, customs staff and hydropower workers are also among the missing.

DAMAGES:

-19 bridges and ~40 km of road destroyed.
-Multiple hydropower plants hit (hundreds of MW offline  a significant share of Nepal’s capacity).
-Border infrastructure and villages in Rasuwa and Nuwakot heavily damaged. Mud is metres deep in places.

text:
Delay by Customs in re-assessing Bills of Entry and generating correct IGST challans: Bombay High Court directs Department to complete time-bound re-assessment within eight weeks with interim protection from coercive action.

Issue:
Whether the Department could be directed under writ jurisdiction to carry out re-assessment of six Bills of Entry, issue correct Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) payable challans, and grant an upfront waiver of statutory interest.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, re-assessment of imported goods and determination of applicable duty/tax liability must be conducted by the proper officer in accordance with binding judicial precedents laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Courts. Ancillary statutory levies such as interest fall within the realm of administrative adjudication during the re-assessment proceeding itself.

Application:
The Assessee approached the High Court invoking writ jurisdiction against the Department’s inaction in re-assessing six subject Bills of Entry, generating accurate IGST challans, and seeking relief against levy of interest. The Department fairly conceded to conducting the re-assessment exercise in a time-bound manner, while requesting that the claim for waiver of interest be left open for the proper officer's statutory determination. Adopting this consensus, the Court held that the re-assessment must be finalized in terms of established legal principles without the High Court delving prematurely into the merits or interest waiver.

Conclusion:
The High Court directed the Department to complete the re-assessment of the six Bills of Entry within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order. While leaving the issue of interest waiver open for the proper officer to decide, the Court granted interim protection to the Assessee, directing that no coercive recovery action be initiated until the re-assessment exercise is completed.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling prevents arbitrary departmental inaction on customs re-assessments and protects importers from coercive recovery during pending adjudication, while reaffirming that statutory claims like interest waiver must first be examined by the adjudicating officer.

❌ Azure global services → Need SCCs

text:
IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Delay by Customs in re-assessing Bills of Entry and generating correct IGST challans: Bombay High Court directs Department to complete time-bound re-assessment within eight weeks with interim protection from coercive action.

Issue:
Whether the Department could be directed under writ jurisdiction to carry out re-assessment of six Bills of Entry, issue correct Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) payable challans, and grant an upfront waiver of statutory interest.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, re-assessment of imported goods and determination of applicable duty/tax liability must be conducted by the proper officer in accordance with binding judicial precedents laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Courts. Ancillary statutory levies such as interest fall within the realm of administrative adjudication during the re-assessment proceeding itself.

Application:
The Assessee approached the High Court invoking writ jurisdiction against the Department’s inaction in re-assessing six subject Bills of Entry, generating accurate IGST challans, and seeking relief against levy of interest. The Department fairly conceded to conducting the re-assessment exercise in a time-bound manner, while requesting that the claim for waiver of interest be left open for the proper officer's statutory determination. Adopting this consensus, the Court held that the re-assessment must be finalized in terms of established legal principles without the High Court delving prematurely into the merits or interest waiver.

Conclusion:
The High Court directed the Department to complete the re-assessment of the six Bills of Entry within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order. While leaving the issue of interest waiver open for the proper officer to decide, the Court granted interim protection to the Assessee, directing that no coercive recovery action be initiated until the re-assessment exercise is completed.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling prevents arbitrary departmental inaction on customs re-assessments and protects importers from coercive recovery during pending adjudication, while reaffirming that statutory claims like interest waiver must first be examined by the adjudicating officer.

Court: THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT BOMBAY
Citation:WRIT PETITION NO. 5584 OF 2026
Dated: 09-06-2026

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.
